candidateRows: Beliefs and theories are almost entirely prior to arguments, sharply limiting what arguments contribute to disagreement.
This thesis supplies Oppy's governing account of argument and frames his eventual challenge to claims that any argument for God is good.
At the opening of his presentation, Oppy defines the direction of his case and previews its implications for disagreement and third-party rational assessment.
Productive exchanges of reasons can resolve disagreements even though that work is not accomplished merely by presenting premises and conclusions.
The distinction prevents Oppy's restricted view of formal arguments from collapsing into irrationalism or a claim that persuasion is merely rhetorical.
Feser's suggestion that rhetoric might replace rational argumentation in determining belief changes.
After Feser raises the possibility that Oppy's view privileges rhetoric, Oppy denies that implication and preserves a substantive role for exchanging reasons.
Standards for successful arguments must be established before determining whether Feser's arguments for God meet those standards.
This methodological claim explains why the debate begins with argument theory and establishes the criterion-setting framework for assessing the theistic proofs.
Responding to a request for orientation rather than an opposing claim, Oppy connects his abstract discussion of arguments directly to assessing Feser's proofs.
Debate about theism should not remain at the meta-level because detailed examination of particular arguments may expose contentious assumptions.
Feser challenges a methodological route that could bypass his proofs, insisting that their specific premises and inferences remain essential to the dispute.
Oppy's extended meta-level account of what arguments are and how their standards should be understood.
Feser accepts that some logical preliminaries are relevant but warns that operating only at that level can conceal contestable assumptions and evade concrete proofs.
Oppy's approach neither excludes particular subject matters from argument nor restricts the kinds of claims eligible to serve as premises.
This clarification blocks the objection that Oppy's methodology dismisses metaphysical or theistic arguments in advance merely because of their subject matter.
Feser's warning that skeptical meta-level methodology can avoid detailed engagement with arguments for God.
Oppy distinguishes his forthcoming position from approaches that disqualify topics or premise types before inspecting the arguments that employ them.
Even a generally suspect ontological proof must be examined in detail before one can give a convincing response to it.
The concrete example reinforces Feser's demand for premise-level engagement and tests whether Oppy's methodology permits rejecting proof strategies wholesale.
Oppy's clarification that his approach does not bar topics or premise types from appearing in arguments.
Feser uses ontological arguments as a test case, arguing that broad suspicion of an a priori strategy cannot substitute for examining a proof's details.
No general shortcut replaces examining each ontological argument's premises and support relation before deciding whether it succeeds.
The response establishes methodological agreement on detailed scrutiny while preserving Oppy's conclusion that the examined ontological arguments fail individually.
Feser's contention that an ontological proof requires detailed examination despite suspicion of its general strategy.
Oppy answers the test case by describing an argument-by-argument procedure and denying that one can determine failure before inspecting a newly presented proof.
A theory is a set of sentences closed under logical consequence, and a person's full belief commitments can therefore be treated as a theory.
The definition supplies the formal object used in Oppy's theory-comparison framework and connects actual beliefs to consequences not consciously entertained.
Oppy introduces a logical conception of theory, distinguishes it from an ordinary finite stock of beliefs, and identifies commitments as the relevant closure.
Arguments are useful only for revealing unnoticed consequences of an interlocutor's commitments, after which that person may accept the consequence or revise beliefs.
This is the central restrictive thesis about argumentative utility on which Oppy's broader denial of successful arguments for God substantially depends.
Using contradiction as an initial case, Oppy explains why logical commitments matter and generalizes the point to all previously unnoticed consequences.
Competing worldviews should be compared globally by theoretical virtue, while arguments serve the narrower preliminary role of exposing inconsistency.
The move gives Oppy's positive alternative to proof-centered assessment and specifies how explanatory scope and theoretical economy govern worldview comparison.
Feser's interpretation that arguments clarify commitments and options without themselves compelling a particular revision.
Oppy completes the priority claim by describing disagreement between whole theories and locating argument within a staged process preceding global virtue comparison.
In a disagreement, an argument cannot rationally move an interlocutor who rejects one of its premises, so its proper role is principally to expose inconsistency.
This supplies the central mechanism behind Oppy's restricted account of argumentative value and explains why premise rejection blocks revision rather than resolving the wider theory comparison.

After outlining articulation, consistency checking, and theoretical-virtue comparison, Oppy uses hypothetical disputes and the Mackie argument to delimit what premise-conclusion arguments can accomplish.
The rational force and practical usefulness of an argument vary with the audience's prior commitments, knowledge, and susceptibility to its premises.
This directly challenges Oppy's general limitation on arguments by arguing that the same reasoning can substantially affect some interlocutors even when sophisticated opponents remain unmoved.
Oppy's claim that rejected premises render an argument ineffective in a disagreement.
Feser accepts that isolated proofs rarely compel everyone, then contrasts different audiences and uses both the problem of evil and materialism to argue for audience-relative argumentative force.
Churchland's cumulative case is better classified as comparative theory choice, while philosophical argument quality should be assessed against the strongest versions and defenders of rival views.

The move preserves Oppy's thesis against Feser's counterexamples by separating theory comparison from formal argument and by replacing vulnerable ordinary audiences with normatively strongest interlocutors.
Feser's audience-relative Mackie and Churchland examples offered to show that arguments can do substantial work.

Oppy distinguishes premise-conclusion derivations from weighing worldview costs and benefits, then argues that confused or inexpert audiences do not establish philosophical merit against the best rival theory.
Oppy's exclusion of the Churchland case appears to depend on defining argument narrowly as a fully explicit and formally structured premise-conclusion presentation.
Clarifying the disputed definition is load-bearing because the apparent disagreement about argumentative value may depend on whether informal cumulative reasoning counts as argument at all.
Oppy's classification of Churchland's cumulative materialist case as theory choice rather than an argument.
Feser connects the methodological exchange to the planned discussion of Oppy's response to Five Proofs and asks whether Oppy's conclusion follows from an unusually formal conception of argument.

Explicit premise-conclusion presentation is useful chiefly for revealing absurdity or unnoticed entailment, whereas productive disagreement normally proceeds through interactive exploration of commitments.
This sharpens Oppy's positive alternative to formal argument exchange and identifies the limited conditions under which an explicit derivation contributes to rational disagreement.
Feser's question whether Oppy's view rests on an overly narrow, fully formal definition of argument.
Oppy grants usefulness when accepted premises yield absurdity or an unnoticed conclusion, but otherwise favors back-and-forth examination of what each side believes and what those beliefs explain.
Informal exchanges still embody premise-support relations and therefore count as arguments, even though page-length formal proofs alone rarely settle substantive philosophical disputes.
The distinction reconciles much of the practical disagreement while defending the continuing conceptual importance of argument in the discursive process Oppy describes as productive.
Oppy's contention that productive interactive disagreement does not involve trading arguments in the relevant technical sense.

Feser argues that considerations offered by dualists and materialists can be reconstructed as support for conclusions, while conceding that compressed formal proofs are opening moves rather than case-settling devices.
For any accepted theory, sound-looking arguments to its accepted conclusions are readily constructible, so such arguments cannot usefully address disagreement with a competent rival theory.

This is an independent justification for Oppy's restriction: judgments of soundness inherit prior theoretical commitments, leaving only inconsistency-directed reasoning capable of crossing the disagreement.
Feser's claim that informal considerations retain argumentative structure and can therefore remain philosophically productive.
Oppy observes that a believer in a theory can generate indefinitely many valid arguments from accepted premises to accepted conclusions, but a competent opponent will reject the relevant premises.
Formal reconstruction retains significant value as a clarifying summary of discursive reasoning and can aid audiences disposed toward its premises, even though it cannot persuade by itself.
This defends the methodological role of Feser's formal Aristotelian proof while conceding Oppy's point that its premises and metaphysical background require extensive independent discussion.
Oppy's assertion that arguments from accepted premises to accepted conclusions cannot play a useful role in deep disagreement.

Feser describes moving from change and causal series to a purely actual actualizer and divine attributes before recapitulating the reasoning formally, presenting that reconstruction as clarification rather than standalone persuasion.
When the intended audience is the best naturalist rather than a sympathetic or unprepared reader, Feser's proposed benefits of formal reconstruction largely disappear, apart from reductio uses.
This targets the audience qualification in Feser's defense and restores Oppy's normative benchmark while identifying reductio as a principled exception rather than abandoning his general thesis.
Feser's defense of formal reconstruction as useful for clarification and for readers already inclined to accept its background premises.
Oppy questions the added value of the final formal summary for the strongest opposing theorist, then distinguishes rare contradiction demonstrations from ordinary premise-conclusion advocacy.
Knockdown reductios succeed especially in highly formal domains, so their power should not be generalized to metaphysical disputes whose substantive content cannot be fully formalized.

The move explains both the exceptional success of Oppy's favored argument form and the limits of expecting comparable decisiveness from arguments about theism, materialism, or other substantive metaphysical views.
Oppy's appeal to rare successful reductio arguments as the distinctively useful form of premise-conclusion reasoning.

Feser argues that famous contradiction proofs concern unusually formal subject matter, whereas central philosophical debates contain material that resists complete formalization and therefore cannot support the same expectations.
Philosophical disputes are more productively addressed by comparing the disputed claims and their supporting theories than by concentrating on the formal properties of particular arguments.
This states Oppy's governing methodology for assessing theism: theory comparison and disputed claims are more fundamental than isolated argument appraisal.
After discussion of proof in formal disciplines, Oppy explains why sound arguments alone do not settle substantive philosophical disagreements and redirects attention to underlying claims.
Calling the dispute between forms of theism the real debate does not imply that atheists are irrational or that their position need not be seriously addressed.
The clarification answers a central interpretive criticism of Feser's project and limits what his claimed arguments purport to establish about rational dissent.
Oppy's interpretation that Feser's real-debate remark removes atheists from rational philosophical consideration.
Feser uses Leibniz as an analogy to distinguish judging a metaphysical system deeply mistaken from judging its adherent irrational or unworthy of engagement.
Oppy's persistence principle is not a genuine alternative to the actuality principle because, under the shared analysis of change, it restates the requirement for an actualizer.
This directly defends the foundational premise of the Aristotelian proof against Oppy's principal persistence-based objection and therefore bears on whether the proof survives.
Oppy's claim that a thing's potential to remain unchanged is realized without an already actual cause unless something interferes.
Granting for argument's sake that change is the actualization of potential, Feser argues that describing persistence through noninterference merely redescribes his causal principle.
Successive states of the universe can arise through internal causal interactions without anything external to the universe producing the transition as a whole.
The proposed universe-level countermodel challenges the necessity of the causal premise driving Feser's regress to God and supplies Oppy's substantive alternative picture.
Feser's contention that every transition involving actualized potential requires something already actual to produce it.
Oppy distinguishes local changes caused by interactions among things within the universe from the transition of the universe as a whole, for which he denies an external cause.
The Aristotelian premise requires an already actual actualizer of every potential, not necessarily a changer external to the changing thing.
This distinction blocks an external-cause formulation that would misstate the proof and clarifies the precise causal premise Oppy's counterexample must challenge.
Oppy's formulation of the principle as requiring something external to the universe or changing object to cause every transition.
Feser replaces vague language about an external changer with the actuality-potentiality formulation and allows self-change when one actual part actualizes another potential part.
Even when formulated in actuality-and-potentiality terms, the universe can possess a potential for a later state without anything already actual actualizing it.
This preserves Oppy's direct denial of the proof's foundational causal premise after Feser removes the potentially misleading requirement of an external changer.
Feser's clarification that the relevant premise concerns actualization by something already actual rather than causation by something external.
Oppy recasts his universe example in Feser's preferred modal vocabulary and maintains that a later universal state need not be actualized by a prior actuality.
Oppy's principle of uncaused persistence is merely a verbal and convoluted restatement of the claim that a potential is actualized only by something already actual.
The equivalence argument aims to dissolve rather than merely reject Oppy's proposed counterprinciple, thereby restoring the disputed premise of the Aristotelian proof.
Oppy's renewed assertion that the universe's potential for a later state can be realized without an already actual actualizer.
Feser analyzes remaining unchanged as not having another potential actualized and argues that interference would itself consist in an actuality producing actualization.
A red chair's potential to be red at the next moment is realized by default if nothing intervenes, so persistence requires no distinct actualizer.
The concrete persistence case supplies Oppy's primary counterexample to universalizing Feser's actuality principle and directly contests the regress-generating premise.
Feser's argument that the persistence principle collapses into the requirement that something already actual actualize every realized potential.
Using discrete moments, Oppy contrasts the chair's continued redness in the absence of intervention with alternative potentials that would require causal events such as repainting.
A chair's continued redness depends on contemporaneous structural actualities, and explaining those actualities supports the regress toward a purely actual actualizer.
This gives Feser's substantive explanation of persistence, identifies contemporaneous causal grounds, and reconnects the disputed chair case to the proof's regress toward God.
Oppy's chair example claiming that continued redness is realized automatically when no interfering cause produces a different state.
Feser appeals to the chair's molecular and atomic organization at the later moment, arguing that ordinary and scientific explanation would not stop at mere noninterference.
Oppy's persistence principle does substantial argumentative work but offers only an assertion of causeless actualization, not a genuine counteranalysis of change.
The concluding criticism targets the adequacy of Oppy's central objection and argues that it begs the disputed question instead of defeating the Aristotelian causal premise.
Oppy's reformulated proposal that an existing state continues into the next moment unless some causal factor intervenes.
Feser argues that remaining unchanged means lacking a newly actualized potential and that Oppy's principle simply denies the needed cause without supplying an alternative account.
Persistence without alteration is governed by a simpler alternative theory under which no distinct actualizer is needed.
This directly defends Oppy's persistence objection by presenting it as a competing explanatory theory rather than a denial requiring independent refutation.
Feser's charge that the persistence principle merely asserts his premise false and therefore begs the question.
Oppy distinguishes changes such as blue becoming red, which need an actualizer, from remaining red, which on his simpler account does not.
Continued redness depends positively on the chair's persisting chemical structure and therefore does not counter the actualization principle.
The move supplies Feser's principal answer to the persistence objection by locating an actual explanatory basis for the chair's continued property.
Oppy's claim that remaining red can realize a potential without any distinct actualizer.
Feser argues that continued redness is partly explained by the surface retaining its chemical structure, which supports rather than challenges his premise.
Coordinated persistence across the chair's properties and microstructure can occur together unless an external intervention produces change.
It extends Oppy's objection from a single property to the connected physical state, preventing Feser from treating microstructure as an independent actualizer.
Feser's appeal to persisting chemical structure as the positive actualizer of continued redness.
Oppy says redness and the relevant underlying physical properties persist together, while interventions such as a paintball produce connected changes together.
The explanatory dependence of redness on contemporaneous microstructure means the persistence example still invokes something beyond redness itself.
This sharpens Feser's reply by distinguishing mere covariation in persistence from the explanatory dependence required to actualize the macroscopic property.
Oppy's contention that interconnected persistence at multiple physical levels needs no external actualizer.
Feser maintains that the chair is not red merely because nothing prevented it; its redness depends on its chemical microstructure at that same time.
A coordinated set of potentials for redness, microstructure, and other properties can be jointly realized without an external actual cause.
The move directly formulates Oppy's proposed counterexample at the level of an integrated world-state rather than an isolated macroscopic property.
Feser's assertion that explanatory dependence on microstructure supplies the required actualizer.
Oppy treats the relevant potentials as a connected package already instantiated at the earlier time and denies that their next-moment realization needs another actuality.
The regress of contemporaneous physical explanations ultimately requires an actualizer, so coordinated persistence is not a counterexample.
It reconnects the persistence exchange to the proof's hierarchical causal regress and specifies what a genuine counterexample to its key premise would require.
Oppy's proposed jointly realized set of coordinated persistence potentials requiring no external actuality.
Feser argues that redness depends on microstructure, which has deeper explanation, and that Oppy has supplied absences of change rather than an unactualized positive feature.
The hierarchy of constitution can bottom out at an ultimate physical level, where the persistence argument can be rerun without a deeper constituent.
This challenges the inference from successive constitutive explanations to a nonphysical terminus by proposing a lowest physical level as sufficient.
Feser's claim that microstructure initiates a deeper explanatory regress governed by simultaneous causation.
Oppy argues that unless constitution descends infinitely, it reaches an ultimate physical level at which Feser's deeper-level response can no longer be repeated.
Any genuine explanatory bottom must lack composition and unactualized potentiality, making it essentially divine rather than an ordinary physical entity.
This is the decisive theistic step: it argues that whatever truly terminates the explanatory regress has attributes excluding it from physical science and identifying it as divine.
Oppy's proposal that an ultimate physical constituent can terminate the constitutive explanatory hierarchy.
Feser says a level containing alternatives, parts, or potentials still needs explanation; a true terminus must be noncomposite and purely actual, hence divine.
Physical simples or a quantum field can constitute rock-bottom reality without requiring any further explanation or becoming divine.
It directly contests Feser's identification of ultimate explanation with God by offering physical candidates that allegedly satisfy the stopping role.
Feser's argument that any ultimate explanatory level must be noncomposite, purely actual, and therefore divine.
Oppy surveys descending compositional levels and argues that either physical simples or value-bearing quantum-field stuff may be the final level without further explanation.
Stuff with potentiality cannot be ultimate, while a true simple devoid of parts and potentiality is purely actual and therefore divine.
The move closes Feser's core dilemma against Oppy's physical termini: either they retain explanatory liabilities or analysis reveals the purely actual divine terminus.
Oppy's claim that physical simples or quantum-field stuff can be ultimate without possessing a divine nature.
Feser argues that field-like stuff exhibits potentiality and needs explanation, whereas a genuine simple has no differentiation or potentiality and is purely actual.
